one_liner: LiteSpeed's C HPACK (RFC 7541) codec with 64K-entry two-byte Huffman tables; beat a 2016 nghttp2 Huffman encoder 2.4-5.8x.
what_it_does: A standalone HPACK library: an encoder with a dynamic table and a decoder. It handles header compression only, with no HTTP/2 framing or stream state. LiteSpeed/OpenLiteSpeed use it, lsquic includes it as a git submodule, and Bun vendors it. You call lshpack_enc_encode or lshpack_dec_decode once per header, with a caller-owned state struct and a caller-supplied byte buffer described by struct lsxpack_header (offsets, lengths, cached XXH32 hashes). The decoder returns LSHPACK_ERR_MORE_BUF when the output buffer is too small. The interface is its own, not nghttp2's HPACK API.
how_it_is_fast: The Huffman encoder looks up the next two input bytes at once in a 65,536-entry table (hencs, 8 B per entry, 512 KB) that holds their combined code of up to 32 bits, and shifts it into a 64-bit accumulator. Pairs whose code would be longer are marked lens=64, and the encoder backs up and finishes with the byte-at-a-time loop. The Huffman decoder uses a 65,536-entry table (hdecs, 256 KB) indexed by 16 input bits that emits 1-3 bytes per lookup. It falls back to the classic 4-bit state-machine decoder for codes longer than 16 bits. Static-table matching hashes the name and the name+value with XXH32 (seed found by bin/find-xxh.c and shared with ls-qpack) into 512-slot index arrays. The dynamic table is two chained hash tables (by name and by name+value). The decoder can also hand those hashes and ready-made 'name: value\r\n' lines to the caller, so a proxy can skip rehashing and reformatting.
when_to_use: You are building an HTTP/2 server, proxy or client in C/C++ that already handles framing and needs only HPACK. This is the codec shipped in LiteSpeed/OpenLiteSpeed and lsquic and vendored by Bun.

Your headers carry medium or long Huffman-coded values (tokens, cookies, base64 debug headers). On an 88-byte x-fb-debug value and on prose, the two-byte table ran 1.7-2.1x faster than ls-hpack's own byte-at-a-time encoder (derived from the post's numbers).
You proxy HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1. With the defaults, the decoder writes 'name: value\r\n' straight into your buffer and fills in XXH32 name and name+value hashes that the encoder (or ls-qpack) can reuse.
You are on a 64-bit target with cache to spare. The 64-bit build flushes 8 output bytes per step; 32-bit builds take a 4-byte path.
when_not_to_use: You need a full HTTP/2 stack. ls-hpack does HPACK only: framing, flow control and RFC 9113 field-name validation must come from elsewhere. The maintainer says in #22 that validation does not belong in ls-hpack.

Memory or L2 cache is tight. The default build carries 768 KB of read-only Huffman tables (512 KB encoder + 256 KB decoder). The CMake MinSizeRel build sets LS_HPACK_USE_LARGE_TABLES=0 and falls back to the small tables and the slower paths.

You need the speedup to hold against current nghttp2. The only comparison used nghttp2 revision 0e1d0400d86a (2016). nghttp2 committed 'Faster huffman encoding' and 'Faster huffman decoding' on 2019-10-08, five days after LiteSpeed's post, and changed decoding again in 2025. No re-run exists, and the decoder was never compared with nghttp2 at all.

Your header values are short, or most headers hit the static table. On the 9-byte 'LiteSpeed' input the two-byte table gave nothing over ls-hpack's old encoder (8.67 s vs 8.80 s); the post says strings under 14 bytes see no speedup.

You must run a tagged release on untrusted input. v2.3.5 (the latest tag, and what Bun pins) still has a fast decoder that accepts EOS padding longer than 7 bits, against RFC 7541 §5.2 (#24), plus UBSan-found undefined behaviour (#26). Both were fixed only on master, on 2026-09-13.

integration.form: static lib via CMake (SHARED=1 for a shared lib) or source-drop (lshpack.c + deps/xxhash/xxhash.c, as Bun builds it)
integration.dependencies: xxHash (bundled in deps/xxhash; build xxhash.c yourself, set LSHPACK_XXH to compile it into the lib, or point XXH_INCLUDE_DIR at your own); <sys/queue.h> (a compat copy ships for musl/Windows)
integration.min_toolchain: Minimum C standard not documented; the code uses C99 designated array initializers. CI covers gcc-8 and clang (Travis), MSVC (AppVeyor) and FreeBSD 13.3 (Cirrus). CMakeLists declares 2.8, and modern CMake needs -DCMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5 (#21).
integration.platforms: README lists Linux, FreeBSD and Windows as tested. musl works via compat/queue, OpenBSD via SIMPLEQ shims. 32- and 64-bit builds are handled. Portable scalar C with no SIMD. The encoder table's byte order comes from __BYTE_ORDER/__LITTLE_ENDIAN.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. All mutable state lives in caller-owned lshpack_enc/lshpack_dec structs and the only globals are const tables, so separate instances share nothing mutable. A single instance is not safe to share.

gotchas: A plain `cmake .` without -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release builds with -O0 -g3 -fsanitize=address and LS_HPACK_EMIT_TEST_CODE. Bun's build notes it had to pin Release because of this. The CMake file also has no install() rules (#21).

The compile-time macros LSHPACK_DEC_HTTP1X_OUTPUT and LSHPACK_DEC_CALC_HASH (both default 1) change decoder output: 4 extra bytes per header for ': ' and CRLF, plus hash computation. lshpack.h reads them, so the library and its callers must be built with the same values. Name and value lengths are uint16 unless LSXPACK_MAX_STRLEN=UINT32_MAX.

The encoder expects lowercase header names but does not enforce this (maintainer reply in #10). v2.3.4 and earlier silently stripped trailing whitespace from decoded names (#22, a regression per PR #23, fixed in v2.3.5).

The two-byte encoder table's layout is chosen with `#if __BYTE_ORDER == __LITTLE_ENDIAN`. On a toolchain that defines neither macro, both evaluate to 0 and the little-endian layout is picked, which is right only on little-endian targets.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued http-parsers siblings do HPACK. picohttpparser and its forks, httparse, iohttpparser, zttp and the Puma parser all parse HTTP/1.x text, and Ada, lucid-url and sorug parse URLs. Pick ls-hpack when HTTP/2 header (de)compression is the bottleneck, and pair it with one of those for HTTP/1.x or URL work.
verified_claims_summary: LiteSpeed's 2019 post timed only the Huffman string encoder, with each project's code extracted into standalone C: ls-hpack rev a1f1ea8ce298f against nghttp2 rev 0e1d0400d86a (2016, called through its nghttp2_bufs chain). Runs used fixed iteration counts on four inputs and report the median of 5, built -O3 -DNDEBUG with CPU and compiler not stated. Results: 2.37x on 'LiteSpeed' (8.67 vs 20.59 s), 5.77x on an 88-byte x-fb-debug value (5.25 vs 30.31 s), 4.46x when a backslash forces the fallback, and 5.61x on prose. The same run shows 1.11-2.12x over nginx 1.16.1 and 1.02-2.14x over ls-hpack's own previous encoder; the decoder post reports 1.15-1.96x over nginx 1.16.1 only.
status_note: Actively maintained by LiteSpeed: the last commits (2026-09-13) fix UB and RFC 7541 §5.2 padding handling, though the last tag, v2.3.5 (2026-05-24), predates them. MIT-licensed, and two .c files plus bundled xxHash make it easy to vendor at a pinned commit.
